10-061.r: Sodium lamps light in 360° (LEDs about 180°, directional); sodium light is almost monochromatic, LEDs give better colour. False: sodium lamps outlive LEDs (LEDs last 50,000–100,000 hours).

10-062.r: Fluorescent tube → low-pressure mercury vapour with noble gases (argon, neon, xenon, krypton); answer: mercury and neon.

10-063.r: Fluorescent tube is preferred because it turns more electricity into light (about 22% vs about 5% for a 100 W bulb), but not almost all; so 'none of these'.

10-064.r: Tube light: electrons hit mercury gas molecules and oscillate them → ultraviolet; the fluorescent coating converts UV into white light.

10-065.r: Electric bulb (Edison): tungsten filament; filled with nitrogen and argon (not oxygen, air or CO2) to prevent oxidation.

10-066.r: Tube-light choke coil steps up the voltage to start the tube, then controls voltage to protect it; the starter sends current to the choke.

10-067.r: Electric potential → scalar quantity: work needed to move a unit charge from a reference point to a point against an electric field.

10-068.r: Power P = V × I; doubling both V and I → P' = 2V × 2I = 4P (four times).

10-069.r: R = ρl/A: double resistivity, double length and double radius (four times area) → R × 2 × 2 ÷ 4 = unchanged, so thicker wire is also 10 ohm.

10-070.r: When n identical drops (potential V each) merge: big radius R = n^(1/3) r, charge nq → potential of big drop = n^(2/3) V.

10-071.r: Field at coil centre B = μ0NI/2r = 4π × 10⁻⁷ × 100 × 1 ÷ (2 × 0.1) = 2π × 10⁻⁴ ≈ 6.28 × 10⁻⁴ T.

10-072.r: Transformer steps voltage up or down (A true) but works only with AC, not DC (R false).

10-073.r: Transformer → steps AC voltage up or down; AC in the primary coil induces voltage in the secondary coil.
10-073.t: Don't confuse: a transformer does not convert AC to DC or DC to AC; it only changes AC voltage.

10-075.r: Mobile phone charger → step-down transformer: brings 220 V AC down to about 9–10 V, then converts AC to DC.

10-076.r: Correct pairs: generator → mechanical to electrical; motor → electrical to mechanical. Wrong: diesel engine (compression heat ignites fuel), solar cell (sunlight → electricity).

10-077.r: AC is produced by a dynamo (AC dynamo or alternator: coil rotating in a magnetic field); a commutator in a DC dynamo gives DC.

10-078.r: AC generator → slip rings; DC generator → commutator (reverses the voltage every half cycle).

10-079.r: AC is not used to charge storage batteries; they need DC, obtained from AC through a rectifier.

10-080.r: Rectifier → AC to DC; inverter → DC to AC; transformer → supplies AC at different voltages to appliances.
10-080.t: Don't swap rectifier (AC → DC) with inverter (DC → AC).

10-082.r: India's grid runs at 50 Hz (±0.5 Hz allowed), not 60 Hz (R false); distribution companies bill consumption in kWh (A true).

10-083.r: Book: replacing diesel train engines with electric ones → only argument I is strong (diesel engines cause much pollution); 'India lacks electricity' is weak.

10-084.r: Power rating, ascending: fan < television < electric press (iron) < electric kettle.

10-085.r: Earth's magnetic field comes from electric currents in its conducting core, driven by convection of escaping heat (not a huge central magnet).

10-086.r: Artificial satellites get electricity from solar (photovoltaic) cells, which turn sunlight into electricity by the photovoltaic effect.

10-087.r: Space-based solar power: collected by orbiting satellites, beamed at 2.45 GHz to rectennas; 99% uninterrupted, so APJ Abdul Kalam urged it as a national goal (A, R true).

10-088.r: Only 1 true: photovoltaics turn light directly into electricity; solar thermal makes heat for power. False: PV gives DC (not AC); India does make PV (2000 MW, 2013).

10-089.r: Solar power can run both surface and submersible pumps, and both centrifugal and piston (reciprocating) pumps → both statements false.

10-090.r: Solar cells use silicon (crystalline mono/poly or thin film); about 90% of solar cells on the market are silicon.

10-091.r: Photovoltaic cells = solar cells: they turn solar (light) energy into electricity by the photovoltaic effect; silicon is the main material.

10-094.r: Photoelectric cell → converts light energy into electric energy; photoelectric effect discovered by Heinrich Hertz in 1887.

10-095.r: Book: photovoltaic (solar) cell is the photoelectric device most suited to digital uses (powers satellite communication); a photodiode only switches with light, generating no electricity.

10-096.r: Net metering → billing system that credits solar (rooftop PV) owners for electricity they add to the grid; the meter runs backwards.

10-097.r: Both false: India is not a leading silicon wafer maker (China, Taiwan, South Korea lead, 2024); solar tariffs are set by CERC and SERCs, not SECI.

10-098.r: Distributed energy resources (small, near the user): rooftop solar PV, battery storage, biomass generators, fuel cells, wind units, mini-hydro → all four.

10-099.r: EV lithium-ion battery cathode → lithium, nickel, cobalt (NMC) or LFP; graphite forms the anode → three of the four.
10-099.t: Don't put graphite in the cathode; it is the anode material.

10-100.r: Alternative powertrain vehicles (not only petrol/diesel engines): battery electric, hydrogen fuel cell and fuel cell–electric hybrid → all three.

10-101.r: Pumped-storage hydropower → long-duration energy storage: surplus power pumps water uphill; it flows down through turbines when demand rises, like a giant battery.

10-102.r: Not true: India's wind capacity is about 56.09 GW (31 March 2026), not 400 GW. India is 4th (after China, USA, Germany); Gujarat has maximum potential.

10-103.r: Not correct: Madhya Pradesh is seventh (not third) in wind capacity. By 2026 Gujarat leads (27.89%), ahead of Tamil Nadu (21.65%).

11-001.r: Conductor → many free electrons, low resistance, high thermal conductivity.

11-002.r: Best electrical conductor → silver, then copper, aluminium and iron.
11-002.h: Silver > Copper > Aluminium > Iron: "Some Cats Avoid Ice".

11-005.r: Salt water, orange juice and lemon juice all conduct electricity (ions, salts, acids) → none is a bad conductor.

11-006.r: Lightning conductors use copper, not iron: copper conducts electricity better and does not oxidise or rust easily (A, R true; R explains A).

11-007.r: Temperature difference along one conductor creates a potential difference; heat is absorbed or released when current flows → Thomson effect.

11-008.r: Closed car is safe from lightning: it acts as a hollow conductor (Faraday cage), and charge inside a closed conductor is zero (A, R true; R explains A).

11-009.r: Ultra-high-speed switching circuits → tunnel diode (quantum tunnelling; negative resistance).

11-010.r: Superconductor → zero electrical resistance and (book) zero permeability.

11-011.r: Superconductivity at room temperature would save billions of rupees: electric transmission without power loss.

11-012.r: Highest superconducting temperature (book): lanthanum decahydride, about 250–260 K at 168–180 GPa (2019); superconductivity was found in 1911 near absolute zero (–273.15°C).
11-012.c: When asked (2013), the accepted record at normal pressure was about 133 K (a mercury-based cuprate), option (b). Lanthanum hydride reached about 250–260 K only in 2019, under enormous pressure.

11-013.r: High-temperature superconductors → ceramic oxides (Hg/Tl, Ba, Ca, copper oxide); reported 1993, transition temperature 94–135 K.

11-014.r: At 0 K (absolute zero) a semiconductor (germanium, silicon) acts as a perfect insulator → conductivity zero.

11-015.r: On heating, a semiconductor's resistance decreases: more electrons are freed, so more carriers (negative temperature coefficient).

11-017.r: Conduction in a semiconductor → by both free electrons and holes (created when heat breaks covalent bonds).

11-018.r: Electron–hole pairs come from thermal excitation, impact ionisation and photo-excitation; impurity injection (doping) does not create them.

11-019.r: At absolute zero a semiconductor's conductivity is zero → resistance is infinite (behaves like an insulator).

11-020.r: Transistors use the semiconductors germanium and silicon; silicon is the most common material.

11-023.r: Semiconductors → silicon and germanium (four valence electrons each); quartz and ceramics are not. Silicon is preferred as it works at higher temperatures.

11-026.r: India banned export of burnt coal (Jhama) because it holds recoverable germanium, used in transistors; germanium also comes from zinc smelting.

12-001.r: Not matched: transuranic synthesis → Glenn T. Seaborg, not Enrico Fermi. Meson → Hideki Yukawa (1935); positron → C.D. Anderson (1932); stellar energy → H.A. Bethe (1938).

12-002.r: Not correct: splitting a nucleus is fission, not fusion. Correct: Darwin → evolution; dry ice → solid carbon dioxide; Graham Bell → telephone.

12-003.r: Book: Rutherford told the Royal Society man would never get nuclear energy, sure Einstein's mass–energy law would fail (A and R true, R explains A).

12-004.r: Microwave photons: Gunter Nimtz and Alfons Stahlhofen (Koblenz, Germany) claimed to push them faster than light, against Einstein's special relativity.

12-005.r: Cyclotron accelerates charged particles (protons, deuterons, alpha particles) to very high speed; not neutrons.

12-006.r: Scintillation counter detects ionising radiation (light pulses in a scintillator) → can check gamma-emitting isotopes in drinking water.

12-007.r: Sun and stars get energy from nuclear fusion: hydrogen fuses into helium in the core; gravitational contraction also supplies energy.

12-012.r: Reactor (atomic pile) uses U-235/Pu-239; chain reaction sustains because each fission frees more neutrons and graphite/heavy water slows fast neutrons (statements 1, 3).

12-014.r: Fission → nuclear reactors, atom bombs, neutron-induced reactions; energy in stars comes from fusion, not fission.

12-015.r: Fusion reactors fuse light nuclei (not fission of heavy nuclei); usually Tokamak design; very high temperature (thermonuclear) → ii and iii.

12-016.r: Nuclear reactor → controlled (moderated) chain reaction for peaceful use; atom bomb → uncontrolled chain reaction.

12-017.r: Radioactivity is a nuclear property (unstable nuclei emit alpha, beta, gamma rays); hydrogen bomb works on fusion, not fission → only 1.

12-018.r: Monazite: radioactive phosphate, India's main source of rare earths and thorium; only government bodies (IREL) process/export it; not in all coastal sands → 1, 2, 4.

12-019.r: India's abundant nuclear fuel → thorium; monazite (its main source) is estimated at 13.15 million tonnes (DAE).

12-021.r: Thorium over uranium: about 3 times more abundant, more energy per unit mass mined, less harmful waste (no plutonium-type transuranics) → all three.

12-022.r: Statement-I true: India relies on coal (thermal about 43.5% of capacity) despite uranium deposits. Statement-II false: power reactors use 3–5% enriched U-235, not 60%.

12-023.r: Cadmium is not a nuclear fuel; it absorbs neutrons and is used in control rods. Fuels: thorium, plutonium, uranium.

12-024.r: Chromium has no link with atomic power; monazite → thorium ore; beryllium oxide → reactor moderator.

12-025.r: Helium (inert gas) is not a nuclear fuel; radioactive uranium, thorium and radium can be (book).

12-026.r: Calcium and lead are not nuclear fuels; fuels: uranium-235, plutonium-239, and thorium (bred into uranium-233).

12-028.r: Atom bomb → nuclear fission (enriched uranium or plutonium); hydrogen (thermonuclear) bomb → fusion.

12-030.r: Hydrogen bomb → uncontrolled nuclear fusion of hydrogen isotopes deuterium and tritium into helium; atom bomb → fission of uranium.
12-030.t: Don't confuse: A-bomb = fission; H-bomb = fusion.

12-032.r: Hydrogen bomb → Edward Teller, 'father of the hydrogen bomb' (born 1908, Hungary); first US fusion bomb test November 1952 at Eniwetok.

12-033.r: Enriched uranium → natural uranium whose U-235 share is raised artificially by isotope separation.

12-034.r: Uranium decays through a long radioactive chain until stable lead forms.

12-035.r: Half-life 4 months: 3/4 decayed means 1/4 left = two half-lives → 2 × 4 = 8 months.

12-037.r: Half-life 10 days: after 20 days 1/4 remains, so 3/4 (75%) has decayed.

12-038.r: Zirconium (atomic number 40) is not radioactive; astatine (85), francium (87) and tritium (hydrogen isotope) are. Elements above 80 are generally radioactive.

12-039.r: Nuclear power plants use U-235; natural uranium has only about 0.7% U-235, reactors need 3–5% (enrichment).

12-040.r: Uranium produces electricity in nuclear plants: 1 kg U-235 ≈ 20 terajoules ≈ 1500 tons of coal.

12-041.r: Radioactive substances emit alpha, beta and gamma rays (invisible) as unstable nuclei turn into stable ones.

12-042.r: Without control rods the chain reaction would go out of control; rods are made of boron, silver, indium, cadmium.

12-043.r: India's first nuclear power plant → Tarapur (Palghar, Maharashtra), operational 1969; original capacity 320 MW (160 × 2).

12-044.r: India's first atomic power station → Tarapur (1969); Apsara (1956) and Cirus (1960) at BARC Trombay were only research reactors.
12-044.t: Don't pick BARC: its Apsara and Cirus were research reactors, not power stations.

12-045.r: BARC Director: Dr Ratan Kumar Sinha (19 May 2010–19 June 2012) at question time; Vivek Bhasin since 15 September 2023.
12-045.c: The book gives no single answer (*) because the post has changed; at the time it was R.K. Sinha (option b).

12-046.r: Dhruva, Purnima, Cirus → Indian research reactors; Cirus from Canada (1960, shut 2010); Dhruva 100 MW on indigenous natural uranium.

12-047.r: Indian reactors mainly use natural uranium (about 99.284% U-238, 0.7% U-235); book's answer: U-238.

12-048.r: Shivanasamudra → hydel power (Kaveri, 1902, Karnataka's first); Kalpakkam → nuclear energy (Tamil Nadu).

12-049.r: Kalpakkam (Tamil Nadu) → nuclear plants: Madras Atomic Power Station, Indira Gandhi Centre for Atomic Research (1971), 500 MWe Prototype Fast Breeder Reactor.

12-051.r: Fast Breeder Test Reactor, Kalpakkam: plutonium–uranium carbide fuel (answer plutonium); based on French Rhapsody; went critical 18 October 1985.

12-052.r: Kalpakkam Fast Breeder Test Reactor coolant → liquid sodium (reacts with air or water); fuel uranium–plutonium mixed carbide; running since 1985.
12-052.h: Fast breeder is cooled by sodium, not water.

12-053.r: Kalpakkam fast breeder (PFBR): 500 MWe, so over 200 MW; fuel mixed uranium (U-238)–plutonium oxide, not carbide; the 13 MWe FBTR uses carbide (book: 1 and 3).

12-054.r: Not matched: Harishchandra Research Institute (maths, theoretical physics) is in Prayagraj, not Chennai. IGCAR → Kalpakkam; AMD → Hyderabad; Saha Institute → Kolkata.

12-055.r: All four under Department of Atomic Energy: AMD (Hyderabad), Heavy Water Board (Mumbai), Indian Rare Earths (Mumbai), Uranium Corporation (Jaduguda, Jharkhand).
hi: Department of Atomic Energy (परमाणु ऊर्जा विभाग)

12-056.r: Heavy Water Board at Trombay (Mumbai) runs heavy water production; plants at Tuticorin, Kota, Baroda, Thal, Talcher, Manuguru, Hazira.

12-057.r: Kalpakkam → Tamil Nadu; Narora → Uttar Pradesh (Bulandshahar, on Ganga); Kakrapara → Gujarat (near Surat); Trombay → Maharashtra (Mumbai, BARC).

12-058.r: Kudankulam → Tamil Nadu; Kakrapar → Gujarat; Kaiga → Karnataka; Rawatbhata → Rajasthan.

12-059.r: Not matched: Rajasthan Atomic Power Station is at Rawatbhata (Kota), not Udaipur. Narora → UP; Madras plant → Kalpakkam; Kaiga → Karnataka.

12-060.r: Not matched: Kaiga is in Uttara Kannada, Karnataka, not Tamil Nadu. Kalpakkam → Tamil Nadu; Kakrapar → Gujarat; Narora → UP.

12-061.r: Atomic power plants: Narora (Bulandshahar, UP) and Kalpakkam (about 80 km south of Chennai), each with two 220 MWe units; not Ghatshila or Nangal.

12-062.r: Narora (UP) → seismic zone IV; Kalpakkam → zone II; Kaiga and Tarapur → zone III.

12-063.r: Kaiga (Karnataka, on Kali river): its second 220 MWe unit was dedicated in March 2000 → the 'recently active' plant; now four 220 MWe units.

12-064.r: Kudankulam (Tamil Nadu): six Russian units in all (two of 1000 MWe in phase one, four more under the December 2008 India–Russia agreement).

12-065.r: Heavy water (D2O) is a moderator: slows neutrons so the chain reaction continues; ordinary water (H2O), graphite and beryllium oxide also moderate.

12-070.r: Fast breeder reactor → makes electricity by fission and produces more fissile material than it burns.

12-072.r: NPCIL could sell Pressurised Heavy Water Reactors of 220 MWe or 540 MWe (Srikumar Banerjee, IAEA general meeting, Vienna, 2010).
12-072.c: The book gives no single answer (*): the actual sizes, 220 MWe or 540 MWe, are not among the options.

12-073.r: Largest installed nuclear capacity → Kudankulam (2000 MWe); Kakrapar 1840, Tarapur 1400, Kaiga 880 MWe.

12-074.r: Installed capacity (end-March 2026): Kudankulam 2000 MWe (highest), Kakrapar 1840, Rawatbhata 1780, Tarapur 1400, Kaiga 880; India total 8780 MWe.

12-075.r: Nuclear power is India's fourth-largest source: about 3% of generation in the question period; end-March 2026: 24 reactors, 8780 MWe ≈ 1.65% of installed capacity.
12-075.c: The book gives no single answer (*), though its explanation puts nuclear's share at about 3% (option d) for the question period.

12-076.r: Manhattan Project → World War II research programme (US with UK and Canada) that produced the first nuclear weapons; J. Robert Oppenheimer directed Los Alamos Laboratory.

12-077.r: Pokhran-I (18 May 1974), India's first nuclear explosion → code name 'Smiling Buddha'.

12-078.r: Pokhran-II (Operation Shakti): five nuclear tests on 11 and 13 May 1998.

12-079.r: 'Operation Shakti'-98 → India's 5 underground nuclear tests at Pokhran, Rajasthan, on 11 and 13 May 1998.

12-080.r: Pokhran (1998 tests) → Jaisalmer district, Rajasthan, in the Thar Desert.

12-081.r: India's nuclear doctrine (draft by National Security Advisory Board, August 1999): no first use, unilateral moratorium, minimum credible deterrence → all.

12-082.r: Both false: Nuclear Security Summits were a US initiative (Obama 2009; four summits 2010–2016), not UN; International Panel on Fissile Materials (2006) is independent, not an IAEA organ.

12-083.r: CERN: world's largest particle physics lab (near Geneva, formed 1954); its French acronym is from the provisional body of 1952 (A, R true; R not the explanation).

12-084.r: ITER (Latin 'The Way') → fusion experiment being built in southern France by seven partners including India; it will not itself produce electricity.

12-085.r: If ITER (Cadarache, south France) succeeds, India could build fusion reactors for power generation.

12-086.r: RTGs power spacecraft with heat from natural decay of plutonium-238 (a weapons by-product) via thermocouples; they are not fission reactors → 2 and 3.

12-087.r: Then: India would not open its nuclear plants to international inspection (A true) but kept the bomb option open (R false); now over 170 warheads (estimate).

12-088.r: Mismatch: SALT II signed 1979 (not 1967). NPT signed 1968, in force 1970; Partial Test Ban 1963; Seabed Treaty signed 1971, in force 1972.

12-089.r: India rejects the NPT as discriminatory: only five states that tested before 1967 are nuclear-weapon states; India (first test 1974) could join only as non-nuclear.

12-090.r: NPT-recognised Nuclear Weapon States → USA, Russia, China, France, UK only; India, Israel and Pakistan are not.

12-091.r: NSG (1974, 48 members) gives members access to the latest nuclear technology; joining does not make a country an NPT member → only 1.

12-092.r: Iran is not a member of the Nuclear Suppliers Group (48 members, March 2026); among the options China, New Zealand, Ireland are.

12-093.r: First country to sign a civil nuclear deal with India after the NSG lifted its ban → France.

12-094.r: India's Additional Protocol with the IAEA (in force 25 July 2014) → civilian nuclear reactors come under IAEA safeguards; not military sites.

12-095.r: Some Indian reactors are under IAEA safeguards because they use imported uranium (others use domestic supply); required by the India–US civil nuclear deal (2005–2008).

12-096.r: ICONS 2024 (IAEA) was held in Vienna, 20–24 May 2024, not on 25 May. India's DAE re-constituted the inter-ministerial Counter Nuclear Smuggling Team (true).
12-096.c: The book prints (d) both, but its own explanation says statement 1 is wrong; by that, the answer is (a) Only 2.

12-097.r: India–Russia 'Action Plan for Prioritization and Implementation of Cooperation Areas in the Nuclear Field' → signed 5 October 2018 (second site for Russian reactors).
